Note: Preferred template (survives editor review verbatim ~15x): 'Here the author/speaker is speaking as if X were Y. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use...' Keep this structure; do not over-explain.
Preferred template: 'The point of this comparison is that just as X, so is Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could ...' Editors keep ~90% of simile notes in this form.
Preferred template: 'Here, **X** represents Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [...]' Editors keep ~87%.

Write only for genuinely abstract/theological ideas. Editors delete ~38% overall - especially notes on common nouns (tears, pain, life, violence, salvation, anger) and on repeated occurrences. Flag a given abstract noun once per passage, not every verse; later occurrences are covered by pipeline-generated see-how / also-occurs sentences.
Content-team mandate: every passive instance still gets a note - do not drop. Historical context only: editors deleted ~55% of these in LAM/HAB poetry before the mandate.
Only write when an antecedent is genuinely ambiguous across a clause boundary. Editors delete ~43%.
Skip for ordinary possessives; write only for non-ownership relations (e.g. 'daughter of Zion'). Editors delete ~61%.
Rarely worth a note in poetry; editors delete ~78%.
Only when the rhetorical force is not obvious to a modern reader. Editors delete ~42%.
Write sparingly; editors delete ~44%.
Apply a high bar - editors delete ~50%; only supply implicit info a translator could not infer.
Genre-dependent: editors deleted 57% in HAB but kept all in LAM. Write only when the parallel line adds meaning, not for every poetic couplet.
Trim marginal cases; editors delete ~30%.

Name notes must go beyond 'The word X is the name of a man/place.' State what the name is: for a person's foreign or alternative name give the relationship ('Belteshazzar is the Babylonian name of Daniel'); for a place give its location or role and the ULT spelling, correcting variants ('Azal' not 'Azel' in ZEC 14:5); for a title that functions as a name (e.g. Qoheleth) give its meaning ('a title meaning one who assembles a group') and whether to transliterate or translate. Editors consistently deleted or reworded bare 'name of a man' notes across ZEC, DAN, and ECC, and removed bare-identification notes for undistinguished persons in genealogical lists (1CH 2, MIC 1).
Context: name notes: state identity, role, or meaning, not just the category; 4 editors across ZEC, DAN, ECC, 1CH, MIC

Note: Existing rule stands: every passive instance gets a note (content-team mandate). Strengthen on alternate-translation quality: name the agent in the active-voice alternate translation. Use 'God' for divine passives ('God prolonged their lives' not 'they were given an extension of life'), the named character when context identifies one, and 'someone' when the human agent is unknown ('someone pulled off its wings' not 'it lost its wings'). When one active rendering does not cover the range of the passive form, add a second bracketed option separated by 'or' (e.g. '[grew weak] or [came loose]'). Editors across DAN and AMO consistently rewrote agent-vague active alternates into agent-named ones.
Context: AT quality: name the agent (God / character / someone); add a second AT option when one is too narrow; DAN+AMO, 2 editors

Note: Existing rule stands: write when an antecedent is genuinely ambiguous. Two further triggers that editors consistently added notes for: (a) pronoun chains where the same pronoun form (he/his/him/they) occurs in one verse or adjacent verses but refers to different people (e.g. 'he' for Nebuchadnezzar and 'he' for God in the same verse), or where a singular 'you/your' addresses a city or nation ('your plunder' addressed to Jerusalem); clarify the referents and give an AT that makes them explicit. (b) An emphatic independent pronoun stated separately from a verb that already encodes the subject ('I, Daniel'; Aramaic 'I myself fear my lord the king'), common in DAN's Aramaic chapters but also seen in ZEC and AMO; explain the emphasis and offer an AT that carries it. Four editors across DAN, ZEC, and AMO added notes for both patterns.
Context: multi-antecedent pronoun chains and emphatic independent pronouns; DAN, ZEC, AMO, 4 editors

Note: Write a translate-symaction note when a physical act carries cultural or religious meaning a translator could miss. In narrative prose editors consistently added notes for two categories: sacred or temple vessels used in a profane or idolatrous setting (mockery of God, DAN 5), and royal investiture markers such as purple garments and gold chains (conferral of high rank). Structure: name the action, say what it communicated to the original audience, cite supporting context in the passage if any, then give an AT or offer a footnote. Surviving template: 'X was a symbolic action by which [agent] [meaning]. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote.' For compact investiture gestures a brief form suffices ('These were symbols of [rank/authority]. Alternate translation: [...]'); give a fuller explanation for ritual acts with theological weight. Editors in DAN and AMO added 13 such notes and most survived.
Context: narrative prose: sacred-vessel desecration and royal regalia; template stable; DAN+AMO, 2 editors

Note: When keeping a figs-idiom note: name the speaker, bold the idiom phrase, state its cultural meaning, and offer two alternate translations, one that paraphrases the idiom closely and one that states the meaning plainly (e.g. '[while under the influence of the wine] or [Belshazzar became drunk and said]'; '[does not respect you] or [does not obey you]'). Editors consistently expanded single-AT idiom notes to two options across DAN and AMO. Classification and keep/drop guidance for figs-idiom is in issue_decisions.csv.
Context: idiom note pattern: two ATs (close paraphrase + plain meaning); DAN+AMO

Note: Write a writing-quotations note when (a) a speech begins in a verse without an explicit speech-introduction verb, or nested speech makes it unclear where a new speaker's words start; (b) indirect speech is reported where the source expects a direct-quotation introduction; or (c) a double verb such as 'answered and said' introduces a quote. Templates that survived editing: 'This is the beginning of what [speaker] told [listener]. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could introduce this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [He told me, ...]' and 'The terms answered and said together introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both terms.' Editors across DAN and AMO added these notes in visionary and narrative prose.
Context: unmarked or nested speech onset; indirect-to-direct; double-verb introductions; DAN+AMO

Note: Write a figs-infostructure note when (a) the Hebrew or Aramaic order places a result before its reason, or background before the main action, in a way that could make readers misread the causal or temporal sequence; template: 'You could put [X] before [Y]. The UST models one way to do that.' Or (b) a verse could attach to either the preceding or the following section; list both as numbered alternatives: 'This verse could go with: (1) the previous section ([ref]). See the ULT and UST. (2) the following section ([ref]).' Keep the note concise and only write for ordering when the displacement is significant enough to mislead. Editors added these in DAN (narrative) and EZK (temple measurements).
Context: result-before-reason ordering; verse boundary attachment; DAN, EZK

Note: The Aramaic phrase כָּל־קֳבֵל (kol-qobel, 'all before', often כָּל־קֳבֵל דִּי) recurs through Daniel's Aramaic chapters with a sense that shifts by context: 'because' (6:4, 6:22), 'therefore / so then' (6:9), 'just as / in the same way as' (6:10), 'although / even though' (5:22). Write a figs-idiom note at each occurrence that identifies the sense in that clause and gives a context-specific AT; do not reuse one generic AT.
Context: Aramaic idiom kol-qobel: sense varies per clause; note each occurrence; proposed in 3 runs, held as single-editor in the 09-09 run

Note: In Daniel's Aramaic chapters the particle כְּעַן ('now') and וּכְעַן ('and now') mark a pivot to the speaker's main or concluding point rather than a time reference. Add a writing-foreground note when it introduces the climactic statement in a speech. Template: '[Speaker] is using the term **Now** (or **And now**) to focus [listener's] attention on what [he/she] is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [So] or [And so]'. Distinct from the hinneh/behold rule; both may occur in the same chapter.
Context: Aramaic ke'an / uke'an as pivot-to-main-point marker; proposed in 2 runs, held as single-editor in the 09-09 run

Note: Existing rule stands (high bar; ~50% deleted). Add: when a key word or phrase has two or more lexically legitimate interpretations that cannot be resolved from context, present them as numbered alternatives — '(1) [sense A]. Alternate translation: [...] (2) [sense B]. Alternate translation: [...]' — rather than picking one and omitting the other. This applies especially to Aramaic terms with ambiguous semantic range (e.g. טְעֵם meaning 'taste' vs. 'command/decree') and to clauses with known textual or structural ambiguity. Do not use the numbered format unless both senses are genuinely defensible; for a clear implied meaning a single AT with a 'You could include this information' framing is preferred.
Context: figs-explicit notes where source-language term has multiple defensible senses; use numbered alternatives

Note: Existing deletion-rate rule stands (~38%; write only for genuinely abstract/theological ideas). Add: the alternate translation in an abstract-noun note must be a natural verbal or adjectival construction in the target register — not a word-for-word gloss of the abstract noun. Prefer idiomatic active-voice phrasing ('to be forced to live in a foreign land' not 'to live forced in a foreign land'; 'And because he acts shrewdly' not 'And because he is cunning'; 'we ask that you would act compassionately and forgive us' not 'belongs acting compassionately and forgiving us'). When the abstract noun is co-ordinated, use a comma before the conjunction in the AT ('what he promised, and acting faithfully' not 'what he promised and acting faithfully') for clarity.

Existing template and ~90% survival rate stand. Two additions: (a) Vehicle-tenor naming: when describing the metaphor in the note, identify both the vehicle (what the text says) and the tenor (what it means) explicitly. Prefer 'speaking as if X were Y' where X is the vehicle and Y is the tenor, not just 'speaking of X'. If the vehicle involves negation, reflect the negation in the description ('speaking as if the rest of the people would literally **not be cut off**' not 'speaking as if … would literally **be cut off**'). When clarifying an apocalyptic symbol-equation (a beast IS a king), prefer 'speaking as if **The male goat** were the same thing as the king' and offer an AT that makes the representation explicit: '[The male goat represents the king of Javan]'. (b) Kinship-term metaphors: always write a note when a kinship term (father, son, daughter) is used metaphorically to mean 'ancestor/predecessor', 'descendant', or a broader relational sense. These are not obvious to translators unfamiliar with Semitic idiom. Use the figs-metaphor supportReference, not translate-kinship, and offer an AT that supplies the literal relationship ('Nebuchadnezzar his grandfather' or 'Nebuchadnezzar his ancestor').
Context: figs-metaphor: vehicle-tenor specification in note text; kinship terms used figuratively

Note: Existing template and ~87% survival rate stand. Add two complementary keep/drop sub-rules: (a) ALWAYS write a note for body-part metonymies where the body part represents an abstract quality (e.g. 'hand' → power or control; 'face' → presence or direction) and for weapon metonymies where a weapon represents the violent act it inflicts (e.g. 'sword' → violent death in battle). These transfers are non-obvious to many translator communities. (b) DROP notes where the material-to-product connection is self-evident to modern readers: a color word used as a fabric ('purple' = purple-colored clothing), or a corporate ancestor/eponym representing a nation where the context makes the reference unambiguous in a single verse (e.g. 'the house of Israel' = the nation of Israel in a straightforward narrative). When in doubt, keep rather than drop — the 87% survival rate reflects editors selectively dropping only the most obvious cases.
Context: figs-metonymy keep vs. drop: body-part and weapon always note; obvious material-to-product drop

Note: Existing deletion-rate rule stands (~44% deleted; write sparingly). Add: when writing a figs-nominaladj note, cite the actual adjective from the source text (in bold) rather than a placeholder label. The note should read '…using the adjective **splendid** as a noun…' not '…using the adjective X as a noun…'. Also prefer the adjective word that the ULT actually uses as its translation of the Hebrew, not a secondary gloss: if the ULT says 'splendid' (not 'precious'), the note must say **splendid**. For the alternate translation, prefer an active or descriptive rendering: 'the splendid heavenly bodies' not 'the precious heavenly bodies' when ULT uses the former; 'powerful people' not 'mighty people' when the context is destructive military power. Two editors corrected the same note for יְקָרוֹת in ZEC 14:6 from 'precious' to 'splendid', and justplainjane47 updated 'mighty' to 'powerful' in DAN 8:24.
Context: figs-nominaladj note quality: use the actual adjective from the ULT, not a placeholder or secondary gloss
